title: Memories that fade and sensors that remember
seoTitle: Memories that fade and sensors that remember | Blog, Jorge Parra
description: A photonic chip with fading memory, a simulated phase-change device and a sensor that briefly retains traces of movement.

title: Light learns to travel, remember and change direction
description: If someone offered you a crystal that splits two polarisations, which colour would you try first? It pays to ask before getting too attached to the headline figure. A modulator has a story to tell about how its film grew, and a sensor keeps a trace of an object after it has gone by.

title: Light on a chip, ions in a pore and spins in a crystal
description: You could look at either end of this pore and swear they were identical. Send ions through and the current tells a different story. Back at the bench, we can also find out where a waveguide loses light and how long a spin in a perovskite can keep time.

title: On-demand photons and two ways to test materials with heat
description: A minute in the oven does a memory some good, whereas repeated trips from cold to hot take their toll on a solar cell. A single-photon source faces a different test of consistency. If you bring two of its photons together, can you still tell them apart?

title: Measuring a spectrum, orienting a monolayer and making gold porous
description: Take away the space a spectrometer normally uses to spread out colours. How do you get a spectrum when all you have left is the detector? At much the same scale, two growing islands of MoS₂ have to meet the right way round, and a few holes change how a thin gold film handles light.

title: Lasers, vision and fluctuating memories
description: People who set up lasers usually go to some trouble to keep reflections out. This team deliberately turns them up. Two other things worth a second look are the noise from a GeTe memory and a detail in fabric that a phototransistor can pick out even when a photograph gives little away.

title: A two-cycle pulse, a light-sensitive synapse and multilevel memory
description: Thirteen femtoseconds is just about two swings of the optical field at this wavelength. Once you've seen how the team got the pulse that short, try the devices built to hold on to something, a transistor that remembers the orientation of the light and a ferroelectric you can set to values between its two extremes.

title: Sensing heat with light and adjusting current with charge or a field
description: With very little acetylene in the sample, the missing light is hard to spot. What if you went looking for the heat instead? Choosing what to measure also pays off in a transistor with two memory gates and in a device whose resistance depends on which way the magnetic field points.

title: A gradual image, a delayed neuron and two twisted crystals
description: If the picture doesn't appear straight away, give the liquid a chance to creep between the pillars. Timing matters when you read an artificial neuron, too. With the two lithium niobate crystals, though, the important decision comes early. Once you've bonded them, it's rather late to change the angle.

title: Light between two metals, power on a thin film and a blue diode
description: One volt sounds modest until you look at the gap beneath the microscope tip. Step back and the design questions change. How do you get power across a sheet covered in sensors, and what can a molecule on a nanocrystal do to help a blue pixel keep its colour?

title: Networks for light and protons, and an insulator with grain boundaries
description: When do you decide which path a signal will take? In silicon you can lay out a calculation before the light ever arrives. In a nickelate each pulse shifts protons and changes what the next pulse finds. In the insulator, the path worth tracing is the one you'd rather close.

title: Mixing light and magnetism, storing charge and watching an LED age
description: Wait until an LED goes dark and you've missed your chance to watch it fail. This team runs one inside the microscope. We'll also get close to the resonators that couple microwaves to a magnet, and to the little capacitor an optical processor relies on to remember its weights.

title: Circular light, memory in a synapse and amorphous regions written in a crystal
description: If a laser can focus inside a transparent crystal, why draw only on the surface? Elsewhere the trick is to choose which excitons to probe by changing the handedness of the light, or to let a neuron turn a flash into pulses for a neighbouring synapse to remember.

title: An infrared modulator, a fault-tolerant memory and a ferroelectric solar cell
description: If your memory has faulty cells, would it help to know which ones before teaching it a pattern? One team puts that map to work. Two rather more literal paths take us through the arms of a mid-infrared modulator and across the junction that separates charges in a solar cell.

title: Polarisation in a film, avalanche in a transistor and a transition in VO₂
description: Send the same beam through a film twice and you'd expect much the same result, unless the first pulse changes what the second one finds. Then we'll follow an electron avalanche through a transistor and look inside VO₂ to see where a conducting path starts to form.

title: Computing with light, switching functions with voltage and bending a compound eye
description: Try wrapping a sheet of paper round a ball and you'll see the difficulty with putting 185 pixels on a curved eye. Which part can you afford to bend? We'll also see what an optical chip needs around it to recognise images, and how one device can take on different circuit roles.

title: Continuous terahertz waves, an ionic photosynapse and domain walls
description: Looking for a frequency neither of your lasers emits? Start by subtracting the two you have. That's our way into terahertz waves before we turn to the ions moving through a photosynapse and take an atom-by-atom look at the wall where two electrical domains meet.

title: Photonics for listening to the spectrum, current for switching a magnet and gold between layers
description: Spotting radio interference after the transmitter has gone quiet is small consolation. Can a chip catch it in time? For the other two experiments, look between the layers to see how a current can reverse magnetisation and what gold atoms bring to an ultraviolet detector.

title: Reflecting polaritons, a graphene gate and dipoles that turn
description: Two wavefronts on a flake, one heading out and one coming back. How would you tell them apart? Direction also matters when you send current through a single layer of molecules, and when you try to turn a ferroelectric's polarisation out of the plane it normally lies in.

title: Shrinking a pattern, separating noise and bringing an exciton into view
description: When the tool can't draw a small enough hole, you can still make a larger one and shrink it afterwards. Picking a recording out of background noise or coaxing light from a dark exciton calls for a different sort of ingenuity. In each case, it helps to know where the signal went missing.

title: A wireless link, a magnetic junction and photons from an edge
description: On a fast radio link, sending a little of the carrier along with the data gives the receiver something to go on. There are two other clues you might easily miss this week, the trace each pulse leaves in a magnetic junction and single photons coming from the edge of a perovskite.

title: Trimming a finished chip, storing states in a molecule and watching quantum dots
description: The chip is finished and the light splits unevenly. Before giving up on it, this group tries a tiny deposit of carbon. Two other experiments reward a closer look, a molecule with several memory states and an array of quantum dots that blink in unison.

title: Growing quantum dots to order, building a neuron and choosing a crystal’s faces
description: If you need thirty-six well-centred quantum dots, it might pay to choose where they'll grow before drawing the resonators. In a blue LED even the exposed face of the crystal matters. And in this week's artificial neuron it takes the response of two nanowires working together to fire a pulse.

title: Pulses in silicon nitride, stretchable memory and emitters acting together
description: How far can a nanojoule go? Squeeze it into a short enough pulse and a second waveguide can turn it into a whole spread of colours. We'll also see what happens when you stretch a memory written with light, and which light you get when perovskite emitters respond together.

title: A liquid-crystal shutter and two ways to use a magnet
description: To dim quantum dots, you can leave the emitters alone and adjust the light reaching them. The magnets in this issue offer two less obvious knobs to turn. Let one fluctuate to explore solutions to a calculation, or tune the spin waves in a flake just three layers thick.

title: Optical cells, deflected currents and light taking a different path
description: Imagine having the array on your desk and still being able to choose which cells act as neurons and which as synapses. Then there are two ways to steer a signal, at the interface with a very thin magnetic film or by writing the path of a beam into an optical element.

title: A flat fibre and two devices for working with images
description: Bend a ruler flat, then try it edgewise. You've already got a clue to how this pressure-sensing fibre works. When it comes to imaging, what would you rather keep, the trace an exposure leaves in a transistor or just the outline of the cell under the microscope?

title: A dispersive lens, a light-sensitive fingerprint and a magnetoelectric oxide
description: That coloured fringe spoiling your photo could help you measure a distance, provided you know where each colour comes into focus. We'll also meet a chip that gives a different fingerprint under red or blue light, and a hafnium oxide film you can probe with a magnet.

title: Polarization, memory and perovskites
description: Once you've worked out how a beam was polarised, could you send it on to the next part of the chip? It's also worth looking after a pulse has ended, whether you're reading a memristor shaped by earlier pulses or a perovskite still glowing after the source goes dark.

title: A waveguide that processes light, flexible transistors and a field-responsive glass
description: On a chip diagram the waveguide is usually the line between the interesting bits. Here the line itself takes part in the calculation. A thin layer also lets the same semiconductor play two different transistor roles, and even disordered glass can hold dipoles that respond to a field.

title: A waveguide open to molecules, a self-regulating neuron and a monolayer laser
description: Why make a molecule travel half the length of a waveguide when it could come through a window in the wall? Keep a clock handy for the other experiments, too. The spacing of pulses matters to an artificial neuron, and leaving an organic laser on for hours is quite a different test from a brief flash.

title: Radio beams, microwave computing and plasmons in a crystal
description: How do you point an antenna without moving it? With eight elements and a set of optical delays, the beam can change direction. Then we'll ask how much of a radio waveform a circuit really needs to read, and why an infrared wave barely spreads as it crosses a crystal.

title: Reflections for reading a spectrum, motion memory and two responses from one element
description: Giving light a more complicated route helps tell two nearly identical laser colours apart. Looking at polarisation with tellurium can likewise bring out an edge a photograph would miss. In between, zinc oxide nanowires can tell you something about the angle of the light even after you switch it off.

title: Writing an infrared image, storing charge and thinning silver
description: All the pixels fit nicely in a drawing of an infrared array. Now give each one a heater and wiring and see how quickly space runs out. We'll also look at a memory you erase with heat and a silver film that makes more of each layer when only a few remain.

title: A shortcut for light, event-based vision and colour from infrared
description: While someone walks past a camera, how often do you really need another picture of the wall behind them? One array picks out what changes. An optical chip keeps the original signal to add back later, while in layered perovskites it's the energy of several infrared photons that adds up.

title: Polaritons along edges, languages in an array and light-activated memory
description: A handful of letters can give a language away. What would a memory need to store to do something similar? Across the lab, a microwire gives away the path of a polariton in the light escaping its edges, and a semiconductor at 2 K responds differently after it has seen light.

title: A nonlinear metasurface, high-temperature vision and an adjustable Hall response
description: At 450 °C a detector can pass current even in the dark. How would you check that it can still see light? Choosing the measurement matters just as much when you want to know what a metasurface adds to frequency doubling, or read a polarisation without writing it all over again.

title: Carrying high-frequency signals, filtering spikes and forming vortices
description: Next time you look at a handwritten digit, notice how much blank paper a network might get away with skipping. We'll also follow the beat of two optical tones into a radio link, and look at how tiny swirls of polarisation settle into a film on silicon.

title: Computing with light, retaining polarisation and turning a mask into an emitter
description: Normally you'd strip off the resist once it had defined the pixel. This team leaves it in place because it can emit light too. Two other things worth keeping are an optical processor's settings between images and the polarisation loops in a film as it's transferred to a transistor.

title: Cavities on a fiber, graphene electrodes and ion channels
description: Something in this device measures just 0.34 nm across. Which bit did the team actually measure? A closer look also reveals cavities on a smooth-looking fibre and a route for ions to reach a submerged transistor while keeping much of the water out.

title: A spin read by light, a magnet that remembers it and a stable dielectric
description: The first paper reports 22 nanoseconds, a number that makes more sense once you picture the experiment repeated many times. What falls out of step between readings? Then we'll write to a magnet with light and look for a ceramic that keeps a capacitor steady as it warms up.

title: Light beneath a monolayer, carbon dots and heat in a ferroelectric
description: A beam can cover a monolayer with room to spare and still barely interact with it. The field needs to be in just the right place. Location matters just as much when an insulating oxide first takes hold, or when heat needs a way out of a ferroelectric film.

title: Infrared in a suspended guide, a reconfigurable transistor and the first steps of crystal growth
description: A scratch on a drying film looks like a mishap until you find out how much its timing matters. The other two teams also get more out of materials they've already chosen, one by suspending an infrared waveguide and the other by giving a transistor a new job.

title: A silicon modulator and two ways to use perovskites
description: When you read an optical symbol, the tail of the previous one can still be there. How much can you untangle before the light leaves the chip? Timing and sequence matter in both perovskite papers too, from the first pulse applied to a memory to the moment an emitting pixel starts to crystallise.

title: Separating light modes, stabilizing transistors and tracking electrons in graphene
description: Mixing two beams is easy enough. The interesting bit comes when you try to sort out their coherence modes again while the light is still on the chip. We'll also look at the company thiocyanate keeps in a tin perovskite and catch electrons in graphene halfway through an optical cycle.

title: Moiré light, memory on two timescales and emission from a defect
description: Two gestures can leave your hand in exactly the same place, so a transistor needs some memory of the route. A snapshot also leaves things out when two light fields form a moiré pattern, or when you're trying to identify which atomic defect in a monolayer gave off the photon you just collected.

title: Light and sound on a chip, stacked transistors and an infrared image
description: Where would you hide a drawing so that a thermal camera could pick it out even if your eyes missed it? In this film the trick is choosing the thicknesses. We'll also look beneath a waveguide to see where sound escapes, and inside a pair of stacked transistors to understand why they draw so little power at rest.
